claim: A PubMed search on 'Drosophila DGRP' terms unveiled 155 results from 2012–2024 (search made in July 2024).
source: Pubmed search on 'Drosophila DGRP' terms unveiled 155 results from 2012–2024 (search made in July 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a PubMed search shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: The Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel (DGRP) consists of 205 inbred lines that are fully sequenced.
source: The Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel (DGRP) was created in the early 2010s and now consists of 205 inbred lines that are fully sequenced, of which 192 are still available in the Bloomington Drosophila Stock Center (https://bdsc.indiana.edu/; Mackay, 2012; Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mackay, 2012 and Huang et al., 2014.

claim: 192 DGRP lines are still available in the Bloomington Drosophila Stock Center.
source: The Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel (DGRP) was created in the early 2010s and now consists of 205 inbred lines that are fully sequenced, of which 192 are still available in the Bloomington Drosophila Stock Center (https://bdsc.indiana.edu/; Mackay, 2012; Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mackay, 2012 and Huang et al., 2014.

claim: DGRP lines are almost fully homozygous because they were inbred for many generations.
source: Furthermore, since the DGRP lines were inbred for many generations, they are almost fully homozygous, which simplifies the identification of putatively causal alleles and elucidation of implicated molecular mechanisms (Bou Sleiman et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bou Sleiman et al., 2015.

claim: The DGRP2 website hosts genotyping data, its annotation, and potential known covariates (well-established inversion genotypes and symbiont levels), as well as 31 phenotypes from 12 studies.
source: This website hosts the genotyping data, its annotation, and potential known covariates (well-established inversion genotypes and symbiont levels), as well as 31 phenotypes from 12 studies (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 1 which provides comparative data.

claim: The DGRP2 website has not been updated for an extended period as the last referenced paper dates back to 2015.
source: However, the DGRP2 website has not been updated for an extended period as the last referenced paper dates back to 2015, and, except for the GWAS computation, has remained static.
evidence: The claim is based on observation of the DGRP2 website's content.

claim: DGRPool aggregates phenotyping data of 1034 phenotypes across 135 DGRP studies.
source: To address this, we created a web tool called DGRPool (dgrpool.epfl.ch), which aggregates phenotyping data of 1034 phenotypes across 135 DGRP studies in a common environment.
evidence: The claim is supported by data collected and presented in the manuscript.

claim: DGRPool enables users to download data and run various tools such as genome-wide (GWAS) and phenome-wide (PheWAS) association studies.
source: DGRPool enables users to download data and run various tools such as genome-wide (GWAS) and phenome-wide (PheWAS) association studies.
evidence: The claim describes functionality of the DGRPool tool developed in this study.

claim: DGRPool was used to study the longevity phenotype and uncovered both established and unexpected correlations with other phenotypes such as locomotor activity, starvation resistance, desiccation survival, and oxidative stress resistance.
source: As a proof-of-concept, DGRPool was used to study the longevity phenotype and uncovered both established and unexpected correlations with other phenotypes such as locomotor activity, starvation resistance, desiccation survival, and oxidative stress resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by analyses performed using DGRPool as described in the manuscript.

claim: DGRPool hosts 135 studies, including 43 that have already been fully curated, 80 still under curation, and 12 under a submitted status.
source: At this time, DGRPool hosts 135 studies, including 43 that have already been fully curated, 80 still under curation, and 12 under a submitted status (i.e. the DOI was submitted by users as a relevant DGRP study not yet present in the database).
evidence: The claim is supported by data about the current state of DGRPool.

claim: 75 studies in DGRPool have attached phenotyping data; 100% of the curated ones, and only 40% of the non-curated ones.
source: In total, 75 studies have attached phenotyping data; 100% of the curated ones, and only 40% of the non-curated ones.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of studies in DGRPool.

claim: The 43 curated studies in DGRPool aggregate 316 M+220 F+133 NA=669 sex-specific phenotypes, for a total of 505 unique phenotypes.
source: In total, the 43 curated studies aggregate 316 M+220 F+133 NA=669 sex-specific phenotypes, for a total of 505 unique phenotypes (~60%), while the remaining non-curated studies provide another 60 M+37 F+268 NA=365 sex-specific phenotypes, for a total of 333 unique phenotypes (~40%).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of phenotypes in DGRPool.

claim: The remaining non-curated studies in DGRPool provide 60 M+37 F+268 NA=365 sex-specific phenotypes, for a total of 333 unique phenotypes.
source: In total, the 43 curated studies aggregate 316 M+220 F+133 NA=669 sex-specific phenotypes, for a total of 505 unique phenotypes (~60%), while the remaining non-curated studies provide another 60 M+37 F+268 NA=365 sex-specific phenotypes, for a total of 333 unique phenotypes (~40%).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of phenotypes in DGRPool.

claim: The top annotated categories in DGRPool are 'Behaviour', 'Life History Traits', or 'Resistance'.
source: Interestingly, the top annotated categories are either 'Behaviour', 'Life History Traits', or 'Resistance', which is consistent with historical behavioral and immune studies conducted for Drosophila as a model organism (Arch et al., 2022; Dissel, 2020; Flatt, 2020; Harnish et al., 2021; O'Kane, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and citations to relevant literature.

claim: The number of phenotypes per study in DGRPool ranges from 1 to 89, with a median of 5, and a mean of 11.
source: The number of phenotypes per study ranges from 1 to 89 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), with a median of 5, and a mean of 11, revealing that, while a low number of phenotypes (usually less than 10) tends to be the norm, some studies aggregate lots of (often similar) phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Phenotypes belonging to the same study (within-study) correlate in general stronger than those from different studies.
source: This revealed a clear trend, with phenotypes belonging to the same study (within-study) correlating in general stronger than those from different studies (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The longevity phenotype exhibits strong correlation across sexes.
source: The longevity phenotype however, assessed in at least six of the studies in DGRPool (Durham et al., 2014; Arya et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2020; Ivanov et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2022; Hoffman et al., 2021) across different laboratories, illustrates that phenotype and its measurements not only exhibits strong correlation across sexes (Figure 2C), but are also sufficiently robust between laboratories (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and citations to multiple studies.

claim: The longevity phenotype is sufficiently robust between laboratories.
source: The longevity phenotype however, assessed in at least six of the studies in DGRPool (Durham et al., 2014; Arya et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2020; Ivanov et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2022; Hoffman et al., 2021) across different laboratories, illustrates that phenotype and its measurements not only exhibits strong correlation across sexes (Figure 2C), but are also sufficiently robust between laboratories (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and citations to multiple studies.

claim: There is a strong correlation between Vonesch et al., 2016 and Grubbs et al., 2013 studies which both examine fly morphology traits.
source: For example, we can see a strong correlation between Vonesch et al., 2016 and Grubbs et al., 2013 which is perhaps expected since both studies examine fly morphology traits.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and citations to the studies.

claim: Three studies (Mackay, 2012, Richardson et al., 2012, and Huang et al., 2014) are expectedly correlated since all three investigate the influence of the Wolbachia endosymbiont.
source: Similarly, three studies: Mackay, 2012, Richardson et al., 2012, and Huang et al., 2014 are expectedly correlated since all three investigate the influence of the Wolbachia endosymbiont.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the three studies and their common research focus.

claim: Females that are more likely to mate with multiple males tend to also produce a greater number of eggs.
source: While potentially conceptually obvious, this correlation suggests that females that are more likely to mate with multiple males tend to also produce a greater number of eggs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between remating proportion and fecundity shown in the data.

claim: 33 phenotypes correlated with longevity from Arya et al., 2010 at a 5% FDR threshold using Spearman's correlation.
source: As a further proof of concept and given society's strong interest in defining 'healthy aging' determinants (Friedman, 2020), we continued investigating the 'mean longevity' phenotype from Arya et al., 2010 and we studied the 33 phenotypes that were significantly correlated with it at 5% FDR threshold (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Starvation resistance is positively correlated with longevity.
source: Among the phenotypes that positively correlated with longevity, some may be expected such as starvation resistance (Rion and Kawecki, 2007; Chippindale et al., 1996; Jang and Lee, 2015) and oxidative stress resistance (Finkel and Holbrook, 2000) but some are less intuitive such as desiccation survival (Rion and Kawecki, 2007; Hoffmann and Harshman, 1999), and certain cuticular components of the epicuticle (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rion and Kawecki, 2007; Chippindale et al., 1996; Jang and Lee, 2015.

claim: Oxidative stress resistance is positively correlated with longevity.
source: Among the phenotypes that positively correlated with longevity, some may be expected such as starvation resistance (Rion and Kawecki, 2007; Chippindale et al., 1996; Jang and Lee, 2015) and oxidative stress resistance (Finkel and Holbrook, 2000) but some are less intuitive such as desiccation survival (Rion and Kawecki, 2007; Hoffmann and Harshman, 1999), and certain cuticular components of the epicuticle (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Finkel and Holbrook, 2000.

claim: Desiccation survival is positively correlated with longevity.
source: Among the phenotypes that positively correlated with longevity, some may be expected such as starvation resistance (Rion and Kawecki, 2007; Chippindale et al., 1996; Jang and Lee, 2015) and oxidative stress resistance (Finkel and Holbrook, 2000) but some are less intuitive such as desiccation survival (Rion and Kawecki, 2007; Hoffmann and Harshman, 1999), and certain cuticular components of the epicuticle (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rion and Kawecki, 2007; Hoffmann and Harshman, 1999.

claim: Sleep duration is positively correlated with longevity.
source: We further investigated the results for an alternative Pearson's correlation test, at 25% FDR threshold (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and recapitulated most of these findings, with the addition of sleep duration (Bushey et al., 2010; Thompson et al., 2020), whose relationship to longevity is complex and still not fully understood (Watson et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations to Bushey et al., 2010; Thompson et al., 2020.

claim: Locomotor activity significantly anti-correlates with longevity.
source: Also of interest is the group of often unexpected phenotypes that significantly anti-correlates with longevity. These include locomotor activity (Magwere et al., 2006), and some other cuticular components of the epicuticle (Nghiem et al., 2000), suggesting that higher locomotor activity is linked to reduced longevity.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Magwere et al., 2006.

claim: Higher locomotor activity is linked to reduced longevity.
source: These include locomotor activity (Magwere et al., 2006), and some other cuticular components of the epicuticle (Nghiem et al., 2000), suggesting that higher locomotor activity is linked to reduced longevity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the anti-correlation between locomotor activity and longevity.

claim: Food intake anti-correlates with longevity at 25% FDR.
source: At 25% FDR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we can also see an anti-correlation with food intake (Lee et al., 2008; Piper and Partridge, 2007), which potentially recapitulates previous results stating that limiting food intake increases organismal lifespan (McCracken et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations to Lee et al., 2008; Piper and Partridge, 2007; McCracken et al., 2020.

claim: Limiting food intake increases organismal lifespan.
source: At 25% FDR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we can also see an anti-correlation with food intake (Lee et al., 2008; Piper and Partridge, 2007), which potentially recapitulates previous results stating that limiting food intake increases organismal lifespan (McCracken et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McCracken et al., 2020.

claim: DGRPool pre-calculated GWAS analyses using PLINK2 on every existing phenotype.
source: Specifically, we precalculated GWAS analyzes using PLINK2 on every existing phenotype in DGRPool (see Methods), thereby considering all ~4 M available DGRP variants while correcting for six known covariates (Wolbachia status, and five major insertions; Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim describes the GWAS analysis methodology implemented in DGRPool.

claim: GWAS analyses in DGRPool consider all ~4 M available DGRP variants while correcting for six known covariates (Wolbachia status, and five major insertions).
source: Specifically, we precalculated GWAS analyzes using PLINK2 on every existing phenotype in DGRPool (see Methods), thereby considering all ~4 M available DGRP variants while correcting for six known covariates (Wolbachia status, and five major insertions; Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim describes the GWAS analysis methodology and is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2014.

claim: The p≤1 x 10–6 threshold appears to be a good alternative for avoiding an excessive number of false positives in GWAS analyses.
source: This may be specific to the GWAS parameters we used (--quantile-normalize --variance-standardize), which already provide a more stringent list of hits than without normalizing the phenotypes. However, in this configuration, the p≤1 x 10–6 threshold appears to be a good alternative for avoiding an excessive number of false positives (Figure 4A), as evident from the distribution of GWAS results across different thresholds (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Bonferroni threshold (p≤2.67 x 10–8) yielded 20 significant hits on average (median = 0).
source: In our results, the Bonferroni threshold (p≤2.67 x 10–8) yielded 20 significant hits on average (median = 0, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) which could be limiting for many studies as it may mask potentially interesting variants that, while minimally contributing on an individual basis, may collectively point to implicated pathways or biological processes (Uffelmann et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and a citation to Uffelmann et al., 2021.

claim: The top variant found in the azinphos-methyl survival study, 2R:8072884 (p=1.966 x 10–26), is a 509 bp insertion polymorphism called the Accord LTR insertion.
source: Interestingly, the top variant we found, 2R:8072884 (p=1.966 x 10–26), a 509 bp insertion polymorphism, is the Accord LTR insertion.
evidence: The claim is supported by GWAS analysis results from DGRPool.

claim: The Accord LTR insertion is annotated as located upstream of the Cyp6g1 gene and has a high likelihood to be the main causal gene.
source: It is annotated as located upstream of the Cyp6g1 gene and has a high likelihood to be the main causal gene (Daborn et al., 2002; Schmidt et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Daborn et al., 2002; Schmidt et al., 2010.

claim: The presence of the Accord LTR insertion is associated with increased resistance to organophosphates.
source: The presence of the Accord LTR insertion is associated with increased resistance to organophosphates, suggesting that derived alleles of Cyp6g1 confer organophosphate resistance in the DGRP (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: DGRP_757 and DGRP_765 generally display lower lifespans in longevity studies.
source: However, DGRP_757 and DGRP_765 consistently display lower longevity in lifespan studies.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: DGRP_852 and DGRP_042 generally display lifespan values around the mean lifespan of all DGRP lines.
source: The former does not however seem to be the case, as shown in Figure 5E. Both DGRP_852 and DGRP_042 generally display lifespan values around the mean lifespan of all DGRP lines, suggesting that they are more likely extreme for other phenotypes and are thus not by definition weak lines.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: There is a modest correlation in the fraction of extremeness across the sexes (Spearman's ρ=0.3514, <1.57 x 10–5).
source: Overall, we observed a modest correlation in the FoE across the sexes (Figure 5B, Spearman's ρ=0.3514, <1.57 x 10–5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The data do not support the idea of 'super normals' or any other inherently biased lines that could significantly affect genetic studies.
source: In conclusion, this analysis showed that while certain lines exhibit lower longevity or outlier behavior for specific traits, we found no evidence of a general pattern of extremeness across all traits. Therefore, the data do not support the idea of 'super normals' or any other inherently biased lines that could significantly affect genetic studies.
evidence: The claim is based on the extremeness analysis performed in the study.

claim: The DGRPool web application back-end is implemented with Ruby-on-Rails (RoR) 7 and all data is stored in a PostgreSQL relational database.
source: The back-end is implemented with Ruby-on-Rails (RoR) 7 and all data is stored in a PostgreSQL relational database.
evidence: The claim describes the technical implementation of DGRPool.

claim: GWAS analyses in DGRPool were computed using Plink2 v2.00a3LM (1 Jul 2021) with parameters: '--glm hide-covar --quantile-normalize --variance-standardize --geno 0.2 –maf 0.01'.
source: GWAS analyses (whether pre-calculated, or using the web tool) were computed using Plink2 v2.00a3LM (1 Jul 2021) with these parameters: "--glm hide-covar --quantile-normalize --variance-standardize --geno 0.2 –maf 0.01".
evidence: The claim describes the GWAS methodology used in DGRPool.

claim: The DGRP database uses the dm3 assembly and contains 4,438,427 variants: 3,963,420 SNPs, 293,363 deletions, 169,053 insertions and 12,591 MNPs.
source: It runs on all available variants in the DGRP database which is using the dm3 assembly (4,438,427 variants: 3,963,420 SNPs, 293,363 deletions, 169,053 insertions and 12,591 MNPs).
evidence: The claim describes the genomic data used in DGRPool.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster is an excellent model organism for studying genotype-to-phenotype relationships.
source: Drosophila melanogaster is an excellent model organism for studying genotype-to-phenotype relationships.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about Drosophila as a model organism.

claim: The DGRP has proven highly valuable to study the genetic basis of complex traits.
source: The DGRP has proven highly valuable to study the genetic basis of complex traits, as illustrated by the many studies that have used GWAS principles to identify variants that contribute to traits related to morphology, metabolism, behavior, aging, disease susceptibility etc. (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A showing the number of DGRP publications.

claim: Phenotypes acquired in the same environment may show greater similarity than those acquired across different labs and conditions due to batch effect.
source: Another potential factor that could explain this similarity is the well-known 'batch effect'. Indeed, phenotypes acquired in the same environment (same lab, technician, reagents etc.) may sometimes show greater similarity than those acquired across different labs and conditions (Ackermann, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ackermann, 2001.

claim: Wang et al., 2017 found that the host's defense to Ma549 is correlated with its defense to the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa14).
source: For example, Wang et al., 2017 studied the resistance and tolerance of DGRP flies to the fungal pathogen Metarhizium anisopliae (Ma549) and found that the host's defense to Ma549 is correlated with its defense to the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa14).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: Zwarts et al., 2015 showed that cerebral cortex and mushroom body size phenotypes are correlated with phenotypes from other studies like aggression and sleep.
source: Similarly, (Zwarts et al., 2015) studied the size of the cerebral cortex and the mushroom bodies (MB). They showed that these phenotypes are correlated with phenotypes from other studies like aggression (Zwarts et al., 2011) and sleep (Harbison et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zwarts et al., 2015; Zwarts et al., 2011; Harbison et al., 2013.
